surrounded by radiance and vitality on every side.
So why has Jane not yet appeared? When companionship beckons,
why does she remain behind within Augusta's boundaries?

yet fail to bring that warm and wholesome flush
which flows through every stirring vein of ours
as we glide swiftly across the open fields,
gazing about with cheerful, happy eyes,

her twilight colors no longer bring us pleasure.

dressed in garments of a fresher, brighter green,

until the meadows echo with their untamed melodies.

never again to greet your twenty-first year—
an age that carries greater dignity than before,

# An Invitation to the Country

How eagerly I await your arrival, dear Jane! Why have you not yet departed from the city of Augusta to answer the gentle call of friendship? Each passing day I find myself wondering what could possibly keep you tethered to those crowded streets when the countryside stands ready to welcome you with open arms.

Consider all that awaits you here. The beauty and vitality of spring are in full celebration now, offering the freshest of air, wide open plains stretching toward the horizon, and a profound sense of joyous freedom beneath the boundless sky. Here one may breathe deeply and feel truly alive, unburdened and at peace.

It is true that April has passed us by, taking with it those tender violets, the soft morning mists, and the delicate colors of evening that once brought such quiet delight. Yet we need not mourn their departure, for May has arrived in their place, dressed in a livelier green and accompanied by the songs of birds that fill the meadows with wild and cheerful notes.

And so I urge you, my friend: leave behind the weariness of city life and all its wearing demands. Come and celebrate your twenty-first birthday not amid stone and clamor, but here, surrounded by the natural beauty of the countryside. What better way to mark such a milestone than in the company of friendship and the gentle splendor of the season?
outputs.L4:
# The Call to Jane

Dear Jane, though distance holds us far apart, this letter comes to reach across the miles and stir the memory sleeping in your heart of woodland paths and springtime's gentle wiles. The world has turned; the calendar unfolds its final page of April's tender green, and May approaches, crowned in warmer golds, to paint the earth in colors you've not seen.

While you remain in Augusta's crowded ways, amid the ceaseless clamor of the town, I mark the passing of these precious days and watch the season slowly settle down into its fullest bloom. The blossoms crowd the branches now; the meadows stretch and sigh; the streams run clear and sing their praises loud beneath a vast and ever-brightening sky.

Come now, dear friend—this is your special year, for one-and-twenty summers you have known. What better time to shed the city's fear, its weary weight, and claim what nature's grown for you alone? The urban walls confine your spirit, dulling all its native fire; here in the open air, the sun will shine to wake in you a purer, sweet desire.

I cannot promise that this bloom will stay, for spring is brief, its glory quick to fade. The very buds that greet us here in May will scatter soon and leave the branches bare. So do not linger; do not let it pass, this fleeting hour when all the world is new, when dew still trembles on each blade of grass and every dawn breaks fresh and washed in blue.

The birds have come; their music fills the grove, and friendship, too, sends out its ancient call. What are the city's treasures, when we rove together through the fields, and share it all? Leave off your cares, your labors, and your grief; the country waits to heal what towns have worn. Come be renewed, though renewal be as brief as morning's mist that melts before the morn.

So heed me, Jane—the season will not wait, nor will these open arms that long to greet your coming. Do not tarry, do not sit within the walls of stone upon your seat. The road lies clear, the way is bright and fair; each moment lost is beauty lost to you. Come breathe with me the wild and fragrant air, and let our friendship's springtime bloom anew.
outputs.L5:
# Now, And, Why

There are three small words that quietly shape the way we live: *Now*, *And*, and *Why*. Though brief and often overlooked, each carries a weight far greater than its size suggests.

## Now

**Now** is the only moment we ever truly have. The past has already slipped away, and the future has not yet arrived. Everything we experience—every breath, every decision, every fleeting joy—happens in the present. Yet how often do we lose ourselves in regret over yesterday or anxiety about tomorrow? To live *now* is to be fully awake, to notice the warmth of the sun, the sound of a friend's voice, the simple fact of being alive. Presence is a gift we give ourselves whenever we choose to pay attention.

## And

**And** is the word of connection. It joins ideas, links people, and keeps stories moving forward. Where a period ends a thought, *and* invites continuation—there is always more, another possibility, another chapter. Life rarely offers neat conclusions; instead it unfolds as a series of "ands." We work *and* rest, we succeed *and* fail, we love *and* lose. This little conjunction reminds us that we are never quite finished, that growth is ongoing, and that opposites can coexist within the same experience.

## Why

**Why** is the word of curiosity and meaning. It is the question children ask relentlessly, and the one adults sometimes forget to keep asking. *Why* drives discovery, fuels invention, and pushes us to understand not just how things work, but what they are for. When we ask *why*, we search for purpose—the deeper reason behind our actions and our existence. A life without *why* can feel hollow, but a clear sense of purpose gives us the strength to endure almost any *how*.

## Bringing Them Together

Together, these three words form a quiet philosophy for living well. Embrace the present—**now**. Stay open to connection and continuation—**and**. And never stop seeking meaning—**why**. In their simplicity lies a profound invitation: to be present, to remain engaged, and to live with purpose.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem in rhyming couplets inviting a friend named Jane to leave the city and join me in the countryside to celebrate spring and her twenty-first birthday.
counterfactuals.output:
# An Invitation to Jane

Dear Jane, the city holds you far too long,
Come trade its clamor for the blackbird's song.
The spring has burst in green across the land,
And I would have you join me where I stand.

The hawthorn blooms in hedgerows white as lace,
The morning dew lies soft on every place.
Leave behind the pavements, grey and worn,
And wake to hear the skylark greet the morn.

For you are twenty-one this coming week—
What finer gift than all that April speaks?
The daffodils have donned their gold for you,
The primrose peeks beneath a sky of blue.

We'll walk through meadows glinting bright with rain,
And I will show you spring's whole soft domain.
The lambs are dancing, foolish in the grass,
The bees are drunk on flowers as we pass.

Come celebrate your birthday in the sun,
Where laughing brooks through mossy channels run.
We'll sit beneath the oak when day grows late,
And toast your health beside the garden gate.

So pack your bags and let the city be—
The countryside awaits, and so do we.
Come, Jane, and let this springtime be your own;
Come home to where the wildest joys are grown.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a Romantic-era style verse epistle addressed to a young woman, urging her to escape city walls for the fresh air of the fields as April turns to May.
counterfactuals.output:
# An Invitation to the Fields

*A verse epistle, in the Romantic manner*

Come, Julia, leave the fever'd town behind,
Where stone on stone conspires against the mind,
Where smoke-grey mornings smother April's breath
And gild the streets with something close to death.
The season turns; I feel it in my blood—
The stirring sap, the green insurgent flood
That climbs the hedgerow and unlocks the thorn,
And bids the drowsy meadowlark be born.

Why linger there, where walls forbid the sky
Its honest commerce with the seeking eye?
Where fashion's clamour and the ceaseless wheel
Grind soft the heart until it cannot feel?
I would not have thee wither in that air,
Thou, who wast fashioned for a sweeter care—
For dew upon the cheek at breaking day,
For all the frank abundance of the May.

Behold, the primrose ventures from its bed,
The hawthorn lifts a canopy of red
And white commingled; every laden bough
Waits but thy coming to grow lovelier now.
The brook that stammers over sunlit stone
Has learnt a music sweeter than thine own—
Yet would grow sweeter still, could it but see
Its silver troubled by the step of thee.

Here Contemplation walks with even tread,
And Peace has made the mossy bank her bed;
Here shall we read no volume but the field,
Whose every page a nobler wisdom yield;
And when the sun declines in amber west
And folds the tired labourer to his rest,
We two shall watch the first pale star unclose,
And breathe the vesper incense of the rose.

Then come—the coach is ready at the door,
The road runs green a dusty league or more,
And April, dying, pledges ere she goes
That May shall keep the promise April chose.
Delay no longer; let the city keep
Its gilded cares, its pleasures bought too cheap.
The fields are calling with a voice divine—
Oh, hear them, Julia! and thy heart is mine.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem in the style of the early 19th century celebrating the arrival of spring, mentioning violets, zephyrs, and blushing May, and calling a friend away from urban life.
counterfactuals.output:
**An Invitation to the Spring**

Come, gentle friend, and quit the crowded street,
Where smoke and clamour vex the weary day;
The fields await thy long-imprisoned feet,
And zephyrs call thee to the blushing May.

See how the violet, in her modest blue,
Peeps shyly forth beneath the hawthorn's shade,
While tender grasses, bright with morning dew,
Bespread the hollow and adorn the glade.

The lark ascends upon his liquid song,
The linnet warbles from the budding spray;
No jarring wheels the tuneful hours prolong,
But Nature reigns in undisputed sway.

What charm hath yonder city's gilded pride,
Its restless throngs, its dim and anxious care,
To match the streams that down the valley glide,
Or vernal breath that sweetens all the air?

Then leave, dear youth, the pavement's dreary round,
The counting-house, the lamp's unwholesome gleam;
Come tread with me the consecrated ground
Where Fancy wanders by the whispering stream.

For soon shall Summer's ardour scorch the plain,
And soon shall Autumn strip the golden bough;
But now, ere fleeting Spring depart again,
Come forth—the hour is fair, the season now!

# An Invitation: April into May

The winter's chill has slipped away at last,
And April's tender warmth has come to cast
Its golden light on buds that stretch and bloom—
A season shedding every trace of gloom.

For you were born when spring began to rise,
When blossoms first unveiled their sweet surprise;
And now you stand where twenty-one years meet,
With all of life unfurling at your feet.

The April showers give the flowers their birth,
And crown with green the waking, breathing earth;
So too your youth has ripened, day by day,
As April gently hands the world to May.

The robins sing their bright and hopeful tune,
Beneath the widening light of coming June;
The orchards blush, the meadows softly sway—
All nature dressed to mark your special day.

So come, dear friend, and join us in this hour,
When you have reached your season's fullest flower!
We'll raise a glass beneath the blooming trees,
And toast your health upon the fragrant breeze.

Let laughter ring where springtime warmth holds sway,
Come celebrate as April turns to May—
Twenty-one springs have brought you to this door;
Now step across, and dance forevermore!

**[Name]'s 21st Birthday**

counterfactuals.prompt: Write nature poetry that personifies the months of April and May, describing spring's beauty and inviting a companion named Jane to flee the city and enjoy the open plains.
counterfactuals.output:
# An Invitation to Jane

When April, with her rain-washed hair,
Comes dancing down the misty lane,
She trails her fingers through the air
And wakes the world from winter's chain.

She laughs in every silver brook,
She weeps in soft and tender showers,
Come read with me her open book—
The pages penned in early flowers.

Now May, her sister, warm and bright,
Steps forward crowned in blossoms new,
Her gown of green, her eyes of light,
Her cheeks still fresh with morning dew.

She spreads her arms across the hill
And calls the swallow, calls the bee,
The city holds you captive still—
But hear her! Jane, come flee with me.

Leave brick and smoke and iron street,
The clamored bells, the crowded square,
Where hurried hearts forget to beat
And no one stops to breathe the air.

Come where the open plains unfold
In endless waves of grass and grain,
Where April's silver, May's pure gold,
Await a wanderer's heart, dear Jane.

We'll walk where no walls dare confine,
Beneath a sky both wide and free,
Two sisters of the spring divine
Shall keep us glad company.

So cast the city's key aside,
And take instead my open hand—
Let April, May, and morning guide
Our footsteps to that greening land.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
